units.name: Food: Where Does It Come From?

concepts.name: Sources of Food — Plants
concepts.description: Plants are a major source of food for humans and animals. We eat different parts of plants — roots, stems, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds. Examples include carrots (root), potato (stem), spinach (leaf), cauliflower (flower), mango (fruit), and wheat (seed).

concepts.name: Sources of Food — Animals
concepts.description: Animals provide us with food products like milk, eggs, meat, fish, and honey. These are called animal products. Milk gives us dairy items like butter, cheese, and curd. Bees collect nectar and make honey.

concepts.name: Herbivores, Carnivores, and Omnivores
concepts.description: Animals are classified based on what they eat. Herbivores eat only plants (cow, deer, rabbit). Carnivores eat only other animals (lion, eagle, shark). Omnivores eat both plants and animals (humans, bears, crows).
aliases: types of animals based on food

concepts.name: Edible Parts of a Plant
concepts.description: Different parts of a plant are edible. Root — carrot, radish, beetroot. Stem — potato, sugarcane, ginger. Leaf — spinach, cabbage, curry leaves. Flower — broccoli, cauliflower. Fruit — mango, tomato, apple. Seed — wheat, rice, mustard.

concepts.name: Nutrients in Food
concepts.description: Food contains nutrients that our body needs to stay healthy and grow. The five main nutrients are: Carbohydrates (energy), Proteins (growth and repair), Fats (energy store), Vitamins (protection), and Minerals (body functions). Water and dietary fibre are also essential.

concepts.name: Carbohydrates
concepts.description: Carbohydrates are the main source of energy for the body. They are found in rice, wheat, potato, bread, sugar, and maize. Starch and sugar are two types of carbohydrates. The iodine test is used to detect starch — iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch.

concepts.name: Proteins
concepts.description: Proteins are called body-building foods because they help in growth and repair of body cells. Rich sources include pulses (dal), eggs, meat, fish, milk, cheese, and nuts. The test for protein uses copper sulphate and caustic soda solution — a violet colour indicates presence of protein.

concepts.name: Fats
concepts.description: Fats provide more energy than carbohydrates and are stored in the body for later use. Sources include butter, ghee, oil, nuts, and meat. The paper test is used to detect fats — fat leaves a translucent (greasy) spot on paper.

concepts.name: Vitamins and Minerals
concepts.description: Vitamins protect the body from diseases and help in proper functioning. Key vitamins: A (eyesight), B (nerves), C (immunity, gums), D (bones). Minerals like calcium (bones and teeth), iron (blood), and iodine (thyroid) are needed in small amounts but are critical.

concepts.name: Deficiency Diseases
concepts.description: When a nutrient is missing from the diet over a long period, the body develops a deficiency disease. Examples: Vitamin A deficiency → Night blindness. Vitamin C deficiency → Scurvy (bleeding gums). Vitamin D deficiency → Rickets (weak bones). Iron deficiency → Anaemia. Iodine deficiency → Goitre.
aliases: diseases due to lack of nutrients

concepts.name: Balanced Diet
concepts.description: A balanced diet contains all nutrients in the right proportions — carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water, and roughage. It keeps us healthy, provides energy, and prevents deficiency diseases. The requirement varies by age, gender, and physical activity.

concepts.name: Natural and Synthetic Fibres
concepts.description: Fibres are thin thread-like strands used to make fabric. Natural fibres come from plants (cotton, jute, flax) or animals (wool, silk). Synthetic fibres are man-made from chemicals (nylon, polyester). Natural fibres are breathable and biodegradable; synthetic fibres are durable and cheaper.

concepts.name: Cotton — From Plant to Fibre
concepts.description: Cotton comes from the cotton plant (Gossypium). The cotton bolls are harvested and the seeds are separated from fibres by a process called ginning. Cotton grows in warm, humid climates. India (Gujarat, Maharashtra) is a major producer. Cotton fabric is comfortable, absorbs sweat, and is suitable for hot weather.

concepts.name: Jute — Properties and Uses
concepts.description: Jute comes from the jute plant (Corchorus) and is known as the 'golden fibre'. The stems are soaked in water (retting) to separate the fibres. Jute is used to make sacks, mats, ropes, and carpets. West Bengal is the largest jute-producing state in India.

concepts.name: Spinning and Weaving
concepts.description: Spinning is the process of twisting fibres into yarn using a charkha or spinning machine. Weaving is the process of arranging two sets of yarn (warp and weft) at right angles on a loom to make fabric. Knitting uses a single yarn looped together with needles to make fabric.

concepts.name: Properties of Materials
concepts.description: Materials can be grouped based on their properties: appearance (shiny or dull), hardness (hard or soft), texture (rough or smooth), flexibility (flexible or rigid), and solubility (soluble or insoluble in water). Understanding these properties helps us choose the right material for the right purpose.

concepts.name: Transparency, Translucency, and Opacity
concepts.description: Transparent materials allow light to pass through completely (clear glass, water). Translucent materials allow only some light to pass through (frosted glass, butter paper, thin cloth). Opaque materials do not allow any light to pass through (wood, metal, brick). This property is important in choosing materials for windows, containers, etc.

concepts.name: Solubility in Water
concepts.description: Some substances dissolve in water (soluble) like salt, sugar, and copper sulphate. Others do not dissolve (insoluble) like sand, chalk, and oil. A solution is a uniform mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Miscible liquids mix with water (vinegar, alcohol); immiscible liquids do not (oil).

concepts.name: Floating and Sinking
concepts.description: Objects that are lighter than water (less dense) float; objects that are heavier than water (more dense) sink. Shape also matters — a lump of clay sinks but the same clay shaped into a boat floats. Density, not just weight, determines whether an object floats or sinks.

concepts.name: Handpicking and Threshing
concepts.description: Handpicking is used to separate larger impurities from a mixture by hand (e.g., removing stones from rice). Threshing is the process of separating grain from stalks by beating the harvested crop against a hard surface or using a threshing machine. Used for wheat, rice, and other crops.

concepts.name: Winnowing
concepts.description: Winnowing separates lighter components (husk, chaff) from heavier components (grain) using wind or blowing air. The mixture is dropped from a height and wind blows the lighter husk away while the heavier grain falls straight down. Used by farmers to clean grains after threshing.

concepts.name: Sieving
concepts.description: Sieving separates mixtures based on the size of particles using a sieve (mesh). Smaller particles pass through the holes while larger particles are retained. Used to separate flour from bran, fine sand from coarse gravel, or to remove lumps from flour.

concepts.name: Sedimentation and Decantation
concepts.description: Sedimentation is the settling of insoluble heavy particles (sediment) to the bottom of a liquid when left undisturbed. Decantation is the process of carefully pouring out the clear liquid on top without disturbing the sediment. Used to separate mud from water.

concepts.name: Filtration
concepts.description: Filtration separates insoluble solid particles from a liquid using a filter (like filter paper or cloth). The liquid that passes through is called the filtrate; the solid that remains is the residue. Filtration cannot separate dissolved substances — only suspended (undissolved) particles.

concepts.name: Evaporation
concepts.description: Evaporation separates a dissolved solid (solute) from a liquid (solvent) by heating. The liquid evaporates as water vapour, leaving the solid behind. Example: boiling salt water leaves salt crystals. Used to obtain salt from sea water in salt pans.

concepts.name: Reversible Changes
concepts.description: A reversible change can be undone — the material can be brought back to its original state. Examples: melting of ice, dissolving sugar in water, stretching a rubber band, folding paper, inflating a balloon. No new substance is formed in reversible changes.

concepts.name: Irreversible Changes
concepts.description: An irreversible change cannot be undone — the original material cannot be recovered. Examples: burning wood, cooking food, rusting of iron, curdling of milk, ripening of fruit, setting of cement. A new substance is usually formed. These are often chemical changes.

concepts.name: Physical vs Chemical Changes
concepts.description: Physical changes affect only the form or appearance of a substance — no new substance is formed and the change is usually reversible (melting, cutting, dissolving). Chemical changes produce one or more new substances with different properties and are usually irreversible (burning, rusting, cooking, fermentation).

concepts.name: Expansion and Contraction
concepts.description: Most materials expand (increase in size) when heated and contract (decrease in size) when cooled. This is due to the faster movement of particles on heating. Examples: gaps are left between railway tracks and bridges to allow for expansion. Liquids expand more than solids; gases expand most.

concepts.name: Types of Plants
concepts.description: Plants are classified by size and structure. Herbs are small plants with soft green stems (mint, grass, wheat). Shrubs are medium-sized with woody branches near the base (rose, henna, lemon). Trees are tall with a hard thick stem called a trunk (mango, banyan, pine). Creepers lie on the ground (pumpkin, watermelon). Climbers use support to grow upward (money plant, grape).

concepts.name: Stem — Structure and Functions
concepts.description: The stem supports the plant and holds leaves, flowers, and fruits. It conducts water and minerals from roots to leaves (upward) and food from leaves to other parts (downward) through vascular bundles (xylem and phloem). Some stems store food (potato, ginger). Some stems are modified for climbing (tendrils in grapes).

concepts.name: Leaf — Structure and Parts
concepts.description: A leaf has a flat green blade called the lamina, a stalk called the petiole, and veins that form the venation. Venation can be reticulate (net-like, in dicots like mango) or parallel (in monocots like grass, banana). Leaves are green due to chlorophyll pigment which is essential for photosynthesis.

concepts.name: Photosynthesis
concepts.description: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food using sunlight, water (from roots), and carbon dioxide (from air). Chlorophyll in leaves absorbs sunlight. Glucose (sugar) is produced and oxygen is released as a byproduct. This is why plants are called producers and are the base of all food chains.

concepts.name: Roots — Types and Functions
concepts.description: Roots anchor the plant in the soil and absorb water and minerals. Taproot system has one main root with smaller lateral roots (mango, mustard, carrot — dicots). Fibrous root system has many thin roots of similar size growing from the stem base (wheat, grass, maize — monocots). Some roots store food (carrot, radish, beet) and some absorb oxygen from air (mangrove).

concepts.name: Flower — Parts and Functions
concepts.description: A flower is the reproductive part of the plant. It contains: Sepals (protect the bud), Petals (attract pollinators), Stamens (male part — produce pollen), and Pistil/Carpel (female part — contains ovule). Pollination transfers pollen from stamen to pistil, leading to fertilisation and seed formation.

concepts.name: Bones and Skeleton
concepts.description: The human skeleton is made up of about 206 bones. The skeleton gives the body its shape, supports and protects internal organs (skull protects brain, rib cage protects heart and lungs), and helps in movement. Bones are hard due to calcium and phosphorus. Where two bones meet is called a joint.

concepts.name: Types of Joints
concepts.description: Joints allow bones to move. Ball and socket joint allows movement in all directions (shoulder, hip). Hinge joint allows back-and-forth movement in one direction (knee, elbow, fingers). Pivotal joint allows rotation (neck — atlas and axis vertebrae). Fixed/immovable joints allow no movement (skull bones). Cartilage at joints acts as a cushion.

concepts.name: Muscles and Movement
concepts.description: Muscles are attached to bones and cause movement by contracting (shortening) and relaxing. Muscles work in pairs — when one contracts, the other relaxes (e.g., bicep and tricep in the arm). Muscles can only pull, not push. Tendons connect muscles to bones; ligaments connect bones to bones.

concepts.name: Movement in Other Animals
concepts.description: Different animals move in different ways based on their body structure. Earthworm — uses muscles and setae (tiny bristles) for crawling. Snail — muscular foot with slime. Fish — streamlined body, fins, and tail for swimming. Birds — wings (hollow bones, flight muscles), legs for walking. Snakes — S-shaped curves using ribs and muscles.

units.name: The Living Organisms and Their Surroundings

concepts.name: Habitat — Types
concepts.description: A habitat is the natural home of an organism where it gets food, shelter, water, and all conditions needed for survival. Major types: Terrestrial habitats (land) — forests, grasslands, deserts, mountains. Aquatic habitats (water) — freshwater (ponds, rivers, lakes) and marine (seas, oceans). Organisms in a habitat are adapted to their specific environment.

concepts.name: Adaptation in Desert Organisms
concepts.description: Deserts are hot and dry with very little water. Desert plants (like cacti) have thick fleshy stems to store water, leaves modified to spines to reduce water loss, and deep or wide roots. Desert animals (like camel) have humps to store fat, can drink large amounts of water at once, and produce very little urine to conserve water.

concepts.name: Adaptation in Aquatic Organisms
concepts.description: Aquatic plants have air spaces in stems to float and carry oxygen. Roots are small or absent (water hyacinth, lotus). Fish have streamlined bodies, gills to breathe dissolved oxygen, and fins for swimming. Aquatic mammals like dolphins have blowholes for breathing. Some plants float (duckweed), others are submerged (seagrass).

concepts.name: Characteristics of Living Things
concepts.description: Living organisms share these characteristics: They need food (nutrition), they breathe (respiration), they excrete waste, they respond to stimuli (sensitivity), they grow, they reproduce, and they move (even plants show movement — towards light). Non-living things like rocks, water, and air do not show all these characteristics.

concepts.name: Biotic and Abiotic Components
concepts.description: An ecosystem has biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components. Biotic: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria. Abiotic: sunlight, temperature, water, air, soil, humidity. Both are interdependent. For example, plants need sunlight, water, and soil (abiotic) to grow, and animals depend on plants (biotic) for food.
aliases: living and non-living components of ecosystem

concepts.name: Standard Units of Measurement
concepts.description: Before standard units existed, people used body parts (hand span, cubit, foot) to measure — these were inaccurate since they vary from person to person. The International System of Units (SI) provides standard units accepted worldwide. The SI unit of length is the metre (m). Smaller units: centimetre (cm), millimetre (mm). Larger: kilometre (km). 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm.

concepts.name: Measuring Length Correctly
concepts.description: To measure length accurately: place the ruler flat on the surface, align the zero mark with one end of the object, read the measurement at the other end. Avoid parallax error by reading the scale at eye level directly above the mark. A measuring tape is used for curved surfaces; a metre rule for straight lengths.

concepts.name: Types of Motion
concepts.description: Motion is the change in position of an object over time. Types: Rectilinear (straight line) — a falling stone, car on a straight road. Circular motion — hands of a clock, fan blades, Earth around the Sun. Periodic (oscillatory) motion — repeats after a fixed time interval — pendulum, swing. Some objects can have more than one type of motion simultaneously.

concepts.name: Luminous and Non-Luminous Objects
concepts.description: Objects that produce their own light are luminous (the Sun, stars, a burning candle, an electric bulb). Objects that do not produce their own light are non-luminous (Moon, book, chair). The Moon reflects sunlight — it is non-luminous. Light travels in straight lines, which is why shadows are formed.

concepts.name: Formation and Properties of Shadows
concepts.description: A shadow is formed when an opaque object blocks light. For a shadow to form you need: a source of light, an opaque object, and a screen. Shadows are always formed on the opposite side from the light source. Shadow size depends on the distance of the object from the light source — closer to source = larger shadow. Shadows have no colour.

concepts.name: Pinhole Camera
concepts.description: A pinhole camera is a simple device that demonstrates that light travels in a straight line. It is a dark box with a tiny hole on one side and a screen on the other. Light passes through the pinhole and forms an inverted (upside-down) image of the outside object on the screen. The image is formed because rays from the top and bottom of an object cross at the pinhole.

concepts.name: Reflection of Light
concepts.description: When light hits a smooth, shiny surface (like a mirror), it bounces back — this is called reflection. Mirrors form images that appear to be as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. The image is virtual (cannot be caught on screen), erect (upright), and laterally inverted (left-right reversed). Rough surfaces scatter light in all directions (diffuse reflection).

concepts.name: Electric Cell and Battery
concepts.description: An electric cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy. It has two terminals — positive (+) and negative (–). A battery is two or more cells connected together. The cell provides the 'push' (voltage) that makes current flow in a circuit. Common types: dry cell (AA, AAA), button cell (watches), lead-acid battery (vehicles).

concepts.name: Electric Circuit — Open and Closed
concepts.description: An electric circuit is a path through which electricity flows. A closed circuit has a complete unbroken path — current flows and the bulb glows. An open circuit has a break in the path — current cannot flow and the bulb does not glow. A circuit includes a source (cell), connecting wires, and a load (bulb, motor). A switch opens or closes the circuit.

concepts.name: Conductors and Insulators
concepts.description: Conductors allow electric current to pass through them easily. Examples: metals (copper, aluminium, iron), graphite, human body, water. Insulators do not allow electric current to pass. Examples: rubber, plastic, wood, glass, dry air, cloth. Electric wires use copper (conductor) coated with plastic (insulator) for safety.

concepts.name: Electric Switch
concepts.description: A switch controls the flow of electricity in a circuit. When the switch is ON (closed), the circuit is complete and current flows. When the switch is OFF (open), the circuit is broken and current stops. Switches are made of conductors but have an insulating casing. Examples: light switches, push buttons, toggles.

concepts.name: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic Materials
concepts.description: A magnet attracts magnetic materials — mainly iron, nickel, and cobalt. Materials like aluminium, copper, wood, plastic, rubber, and glass are not attracted by magnets (non-magnetic). Steel (iron alloy) is magnetic. This property is used in separating magnetic materials from waste (e.g., separating iron filings from sand).

concepts.name: Properties of Magnets
concepts.description: Key properties of magnets: Every magnet has two poles — North (N) and South (S). Like poles repel each other (N-N, S-S), unlike poles attract (N-S). The force of attraction is strongest at the poles. A freely suspended magnet always points North-South (used in compass). If a magnet is broken, each piece becomes a complete magnet with two poles.

concepts.name: Magnetic Compass and Directions
concepts.description: A magnetic compass has a freely pivoting magnetic needle that always aligns along the North-South direction due to the Earth's magnetic field. The North pole of the needle points to geographic North. Compasses are used for navigation by hikers, ships, and pilots. Smartphones also use digital compasses based on the same principle.

concepts.name: Water Cycle
concepts.description: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere. Key processes: Evaporation (water from oceans/lakes turns into vapour due to solar heat), Transpiration (water vapour released by plants), Condensation (water vapour cools and forms clouds/water droplets), Precipitation (water falls as rain, snow, or hail), Collection (water collects in oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater).

concepts.name: Groundwater and Water Table
concepts.description: Rainwater seeps into the ground through soil and rock layers and collects underground as groundwater. The upper level of groundwater stored underground is called the water table. Wells and tube wells draw water from below the water table. When rain is scarce or too much water is pumped out, the water table falls — this is called depletion of groundwater.

concepts.name: Water Conservation
concepts.description: Freshwater is limited and must be conserved. Methods: Rainwater harvesting (collecting rainwater in tanks or pits to recharge groundwater). Drip irrigation (supplying water directly to plant roots). Fixing leaking taps. Reusing water (washing machine water to mop floors). Afforestation (planting trees helps groundwater recharge). Reducing industrial water pollution.

concepts.name: Composition of Air
concepts.description: Air is a mixture of gases. Approximate composition: Nitrogen (78%) — most abundant, used by plants for protein synthesis. Oxygen (21%) — needed for respiration and burning. Carbon dioxide (0.03%) — used by plants for photosynthesis. Noble gases (argon, etc.) (~1%). Water vapour and dust particles are also present. Air has no colour, taste, or smell.

concepts.name: Oxygen and Its Importance
concepts.description: Oxygen makes up about 21% of air and is essential for life. All living organisms (except some bacteria) need oxygen for respiration (to release energy from food). Oxygen also supports combustion (burning). The amount of oxygen in the atmosphere is maintained by plants producing oxygen through photosynthesis. Deep-sea divers and astronauts carry oxygen cylinders.

concepts.name: Air Pollution
concepts.description: Air pollution occurs when harmful substances enter the air. Major pollutants: smoke from factories and vehicles (carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide), burning of fuels, crop burning, dust. Effects: respiratory diseases (asthma, bronchitis), acid rain (damages buildings and crops), global warming. Ways to reduce: use public transport, plant trees, use cleaner fuels, avoid burning waste.

concepts.name: Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable Waste
concepts.description: Biodegradable waste can be broken down by microorganisms (bacteria, fungi) into harmless substances. Examples: food scraps, vegetable peels, paper, cotton, leaves, wood. Non-biodegradable waste cannot be broken down naturally and persists in the environment for hundreds of years. Examples: plastic, glass, metals, Styrofoam. Separation of these two types is the first step in waste management.

concepts.name: Composting
concepts.description: Composting is the process of converting biodegradable waste (kitchen scraps, leaves, vegetable peels) into compost — a rich organic fertiliser. Microorganisms break down the organic matter. The compost is then used to improve soil quality for plants. Vermicomposting uses earthworms to speed up decomposition. Composting reduces the amount of waste sent to landfills.

concepts.name: Recycling and the 3Rs
concepts.description: The 3Rs of waste management: Reduce (use less — buy only what you need, avoid single-use plastics), Reuse (use items multiple times — cloth bags, refillable bottles), Recycle (convert waste into new products — paper, glass, metals, and some plastics can be recycled). Recycling saves raw materials, energy, and reduces pollution. Paper recycling saves trees.

concepts.name: Landfills and Their Problems
concepts.description: A landfill is a designated area where waste is dumped and buried. Problems: Leachate (polluted liquid from waste) seeps into soil and contaminates groundwater. Decomposing waste produces methane (greenhouse gas). Landfills take up large areas of land. Non-biodegradable waste remains in landfills for centuries. Proper waste segregation and recycling can significantly reduce landfill use.
